newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Keep HK free, West tells China hours off handover.
newsitem.headline: Keep HK free, West tells China hours off handover.

text.p: Western leaders urged Beijing on Monday to preserve Hong Kong's freedoms, hours before British colonial rule ends with a ceremonial midnight handover to China.

A joint plea by the United States and Britain came after Hong Kong's future chief executive Tung Chee-hwa set an elections timetable and China's President Jiang Zemin pledged to uphold human rights and freedom.
With Chinese troops gathered on the border, Hong Kong residents started their last day under British rule in a carnival atmosphere of pomp, pageantry and parties.
And a billion mainland Chinese readied to embrace Hong Kong after 156 years of humiliating separation when Britain seized the territory in the Opium Wars.

The mainly-Chinese 6.4 million population of this East Asian economic powerhouse shares a mixed undercurrent of emotions -- elation at returning to the Chinese motherland and concern over future freedoms.
Dragon dances, the skirl of bagpipes, massive firework displays and marching bands were to be the order of the day.

In the Chinese capital Beijing, there was a festive mood. Streets were festooned with banners proclaiming "Wash away 100 years of national shame", and a blimp high over the city declared "Celebrate the return of Hong Kong".

Across the border, in the southern city of Shenzhen, China's top army official told People's Liberation Army (PLA) troops to love Hong Kong's people and protect their prosperity when they enter the territory to assert Chinese sovereignty within hours.

The PLA forces will sweep in by land, sea and air. The United States has joined Britain in sharply criticising the dispatch of 4,000 troops by armoured car, helicopter and warships. About 200 PLA soldiers have been in the colony for weeks on logistics tasks for the arrival of the main force.
"I don't think this is the best way to start off," visiting U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said.

Hong Kong becomes part of China on the stroke of midnight (1600 GMT) on Monday night, ending a colonial interlude that took it from a barely-populated rocky island to one of the richest places in the world.

Much uncertainty about the prospect ahead surrounds the unprecedented handover of Hong Kong, a flourishing capitalist bastion, joining a communist, potential superpower, with considerable autonomy promised for 50 years.

World leaders gathered in Hong Kong, signifying that the transfer of power has become a signal milestone in late-century events like the 1989 Berlin Wall collapse and the 1994 South African elections ending white minority rule.
With the Hong Kong handover just hours away, the United States and Britain delivered a strong joint message to China to maintain the territory's freedoms.
British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook conferred with Albright on the royal yacht Britannia and declared:
"We are both confident that Hong Kong can have a prosperous future and a free future if the terms of the (1984 Sino-British) Joint Declaration are adhered to."
That plea is set to be underlined when the leaders of Britain and China hold their summit before the Hong Kong handover. British Prime Minister Tony Blair will meet President Jiang Zemin.
On arrival at a rain-swept Kai Tak airport, Blair said he was eager to build a strong and stable relationship with China but added that Beijing must keep to its promises on Hong Kong's freedoms.

In the ceremony, Britain's heir to the throne Prince Charles hands over a 400 square mile (1,000 square km) area often described as a "Pearl of the Orient" to Jiang. Britain's Union Jack comes down and the five-starred red flag of China rises.
Alongside China's flag will fly Hong Kong's own new flag, a local flower called the bauhinia emblazoned on a red background.

On the eve of the handover, Jiang vowed to fulfil China's promises under the 1984 Sino-British pact of "one country, two systems" that pledges to allow Hong Kong to carry on with its supercharged capitalist ways in the embrace of communist rule.

In another gesture of reassurance, Tung Chee-hwa, the shipping magnate chosen by Beijing to take charge of Hong Kong, for the first time on Sunday set a specific date of next May for elections to a new legislature.

A democratically-elected Legislative Council, Britain's parting political gift to Hong Kong and the focus of Sino-British feuding, is being scrapped until the election in favour of a provisional legislature approved by Beijing.
Britain and the United States are sending only diplomats, not their main guests, to the legislature's swearing in shortly after midnight to protest that it was not elected.
But Canada joined those breaking ranks on the boycott when Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said on Monday he would attend the inauguration.
